prompt: Before Go 1.22, why did a route like `GET /events/{id}` need a router from outside the standard library, or extra code in the handler?

choices.text: `net/http` had no way to write JSON responses at the time
choices.why: `encoding/json` writes to any writer; JSON was never the gap.

choices.text: `ServeMux` matched neither methods nor wildcards
choices.why: Right. The handler for `/events/` had to check `r.Method` and cut the id out of the path itself.

choices.text: The standard server refused paths longer than one segment
choices.why: Subtree patterns like `/events/` matched every path below them.

choices.text: A handler could not read the request's method before 1.22
choices.why: `r.Method` was always there; the mux just did not route by it.

prompt: Match each project to what it brought.

pairs.right: `:id` parameters matched in a tree; Gin's router began as a copy
regular expressions and host matching; archived in 2022, revived in 2023
handlers that stay `http.Handler`, middleware in the standard shape

prompt: What does a framework bring that a router alone does not?

choices.text: Method matching, so that `GET` and `POST` on one path reach different code
choices.why: A router does that already; httprouter did in 2013.

choices.text: Binding a body into a struct with validation from tags, and a central place where errors become responses
choices.why: Right, plus its own request type and a catalogue of middleware.

choices.text: A faster compiler
choices.why: Every version here was built by the same `go build`.

choices.text: Wildcards in paths, read back by name inside the handler that matched
choices.why: Routers had those long before frameworks bundled them.

prompt: Why was the yardstick API written in the standard library before any framework?

choices.text: Because a framework refuses to compile unless a standard library version of the same API sits beside it
choices.why: Each framework version is a program of its own.

choices.text: To be copied into boxoffice
choices.why: boxoffice keeps its own style; this one is the plain style of lesson 1.

choices.text: Because it is the fastest of the five, so the others are measured against its speed
choices.why: No speed was measured in this lesson.

choices.text: So that what differs between versions is the framework, with the same store, check and statuses
choices.why: Right. Every version keeps the same rules and is asked the same six questions.

prompt: What does `gin.Default()` attach to the router before you register a single route?

choices.text: CORS for every origin and a token check on every route
choices.why: Neither is attached by default.

choices.text: A logger and a panic recovery
choices.why: Right, the two middlewares lesson 2 wrote by hand.

choices.text: An `http.Server` with the four timeouts of lesson 1
choices.why: `r.Run` uses `http.ListenAndServe`, with no timeouts at all.

choices.text: A validator for every struct
choices.why: Validation runs when `ShouldBindJSON` reads `binding` tags, not as a middleware.

prompt: `curl -X DELETE localhost:8080/events/1` against the Gin version answers 404. What explains it?
hint: Gin's router knows how to say 405.

choices.text: Event 1 was deleted by an earlier request
choices.why: There is no delete route; the event still answered `GET` a moment earlier.

choices.text: Gin only supports the methods `GET` and `POST`
choices.why: Gin registers `r.DELETE` routes like any other.

choices.text: `HandleMethodNotAllowed` is off by default
choices.why: Right. Turned on, the wrong method gets 405; off, the client is told the event does not exist.

choices.text: The path pattern `:id` refuses numbers
choices.why: `GET /events/1` matched it and answered 200.

prompt: Gin answered a quantity of 40 with `Key: 'purchase.Quantity' Error:Field validation for 'Quantity' failed on the 'max' tag`. What is wrong with that as an answer for a client?

choices.text: It names Go struct fields and tag names, the server's vocabulary rather than the client's
choices.why: Right. Gin gives the rules for free and leaves the message to you to translate.

choices.text: Nothing: it names the JSON key the client sent
choices.why: The client sent `quantity`; the message says `purchase.Quantity`.

choices.text: It came with status 500
choices.why: The handler chose 422 for binding errors.

choices.text: It leaks the token
choices.why: No token is involved in this route.

prompt: A Gin service rate-limits each client by `c.ClientIP()` and leaves the trusted proxies at their default. What does an abusive client do?

choices.text: Nothing: the limit uses the TCP address
choices.why: By default `ClientIP` believes `X-Forwarded-For` from anybody.

choices.text: Switches `GIN_MODE` to `debug`
choices.why: That is the server's environment, out of a client's reach.

choices.text: Sends requests without a body
choices.why: A missing body changes nothing about who the client appears to be.

choices.text: Sends a different `X-Forwarded-For` on each request and looks like a new client every time
choices.why: Right. `SetTrustedProxies` names whose header counts.

prompt: You keep Gin and want lesson 1's four timeouts. What do you do?

choices.text: Call `r.Run` with a longer address string
choices.why: `Run` calls `http.ListenAndServe`, which has no timeouts whatever the address.

choices.text: Set `GIN_MODE=release`
choices.why: Release mode silences the debug notes and sets no deadline.

choices.text: Put the engine in an `http.Server`'s `Handler` field and never call `Run`
choices.why: Right, the same server boxoffice already builds.

choices.text: Add the `ReadHeaderTimeout` binding tag
choices.why: Binding tags validate bodies; they have nothing to do with the connection.

prompt: How many modules besides the program's own did `go list -m all` name for the Gin version?
What is Echo's central idea about failures?
hint: Look at the handlers' return type.

choices.text: Errors are panics, and a recovery middleware wrapped around the whole server turns each into a response
choices.why: Echo handlers `return` errors; nothing panics.

choices.text: Errors are written as HTML pages
choices.why: That was Beego. Echo answered JSON.

choices.text: A handler returns the error, and one error handler for the whole server turns it into a response
choices.why: Right, the shape lesson 3 built with `fail`, inside the framework.

choices.text: Each handler writes its own error format to the response and then returns an empty value
choices.why: That is the standard library's way, and what Echo moves to one place.

prompt: The Echo version answered the body `{"quantity": "two"}` with `{"message":"Bad Request"}`. Where did the detail go?

choices.text: Nowhere: Echo discards decoding errors
choices.why: The log line carries it in full.

choices.text: Into a response header
choices.why: The headers carry no such thing.

choices.text: To the client, in a second response
choices.why: One request gets one response.

choices.text: Into the server's log
choices.why: Right. Echo keeps a decoding error's text for the operator, the cautious default.

prompt: Which of the four answered an unknown path with JSON, without anyone writing a format?

choices.text: Gin
choices.why: Gin's 404 was plain text.

choices.text: Fiber
choices.why: Fiber's default error handler writes text.

choices.text: Beego
choices.why: Beego sent a 2,000-byte HTML page.

choices.text: Echo
choices.why: Right, `{"message":"Not Found"}`, and its 405 kept the `Allow` header.

prompt: In Echo v5, a handler's signature is `func(c *echo.Context) ___`.
A team wants JSON errors on every route, including unknown paths, without losing the 405, and wants few dependencies. Which version from this lesson fits best as it was written?
hint: Compare the rows of the second table.

choices.text: The standard library
choices.why: The mux's own 404 and 405 are text, and lesson 3 showed a catch-all costs the 405.

choices.text: Gin, because it has the most stars and the binding tags
choices.why: Gin answers a wrong method with a text 404 by default and brings 55 modules.

choices.text: Echo
choices.why: Right: JSON for the 405 and the 404 by default, and eight modules besides yours.

choices.text: Beego, because it brings the whole stack
choices.why: Its default 404 is HTML and it brings 102 modules.

prompt: What is Fiber built on?
hint: Not what the other three share.

choices.text: `fasthttp`
choices.why: Right, a separate HTTP implementation written for speed.

choices.text: `net/http`, like Gin and Echo
choices.why: That is exactly what Fiber is not.

choices.text: `httprouter`, the router Gin started from
choices.why: That is Gin's ancestry.

choices.text: Express, compiled to Go from JavaScript source
choices.why: Fiber copies Express's API style, not its code.

prompt: A Fiber handler stores `c.Params("id")` in a map read later by a background goroutine, and some stored ids change into other values. Why?
hint: Where does that string's memory come from?

choices.text: The map needs a mutex
choices.why: A race would corrupt the map, not turn one id into another id from a later request.

choices.text: `c.Params` returns a random id
choices.why: It returns the segment of the path, at that moment.

choices.text: Fiber restarts between requests
choices.why: One process served every request; the banner printed once.

choices.text: The string points into a buffer the next request reuses; it has to be copied first
choices.why: Right. Fiber's documentation warns of it and has a setting that copies every value.

prompt: Which of these follow from a Fiber handler not being an `http.Handler`? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: Lesson 2's middlewares do not plug in directly
choices.why: Right. Fiber ships an adaptor package and its own middleware.

choices.text: `httptest` does not apply as it is; `app.Test` replaces it
choices.why: Right. Lesson 15's handler tests use `httptest`.

choices.text: The server speaks no HTTP/2
choices.why: Right. `fasthttp` lacks it, where `net/http` has it without being asked.

choices.text: JSON responses are refused
choices.why: `c.JSON` answered the event as JSON.

choices.text: Handlers have to return nothing
choices.why: Fiber handlers return an `error`, like Echo's.

prompt: Fiber answered an invalid quantity with `quantity must be between 1 and 10`, with no JSON around it. What would make it answer JSON?

choices.text: Using `fiber.Map` instead of `fiber.NewError` in every handler
choices.why: That moves the format back into each handler, which is what a central handler avoids.

choices.text: Sending the request with `--json`
choices.why: It was sent with `--json`; that describes the request, not the answer.

choices.text: An error handler of your own in `fiber.Config`
choices.why: Right. The default one writes `err.Error()` as text.

choices.text: Upgrading to Fiber v4
choices.why: The lesson used v3.6.1 and named no other version.

prompt: What kind of framework is Beego?

choices.text: A router in the tradition of httprouter, leaving the ORM and the configuration to you
choices.why: That describes httprouter or chi.

choices.text: A wrapper around fasthttp that copies the Express API for people coming from Node.js
choices.why: That is Fiber; Beego runs on `net/http`.

choices.text: A full-stack MVC framework with an ORM, configuration, sessions, cache and the `bee` tool
choices.why: Right. Routing is one part of what it brings.

choices.text: A validation library
choices.why: That is `go-playground/validator`.

prompt: A JSON client calls an unknown path on the Beego version. What does it receive?

choices.text: `{"error":"no such event"}`
choices.why: That is the handler's 404 for an event; no handler ran here.

choices.text: A 405 with `Allow: GET`, as the standard library's mux would have answered the same request
choices.why: Beego answered even the wrong method with its HTML 404.

choices.text: An empty reply, the connection closed without a status line or headers
choices.why: The body was a whole page.

choices.text: A 404 page of 2,000 bytes of HTML, powered by beego 2.0.0
choices.why: Right, meant for a person in a browser, and naming a version the module is not.

prompt: Beego's log starts with a complaint about `conf/app.conf`. What does it tell you?

choices.text: The server failed to start
choices.why: The next line says it is running, and it answered every request.

choices.text: The routes were read from that file
choices.why: They were registered in `main` with `web.Get` and `web.Post`.

choices.text: The module download failed
choices.why: The program built and ran; it is a runtime notice.

choices.text: Beego expects a project laid out its way, configuration file included
choices.why: Right. A full-stack framework assumes a structure.

prompt: Why does the Beego version need `web.BConfig.CopyRequestBody = true`?

choices.text: Without it `ctx.Input.RequestBody` does not hold the body
choices.why: Right, a setting of Beego's global configuration object.

choices.text: It limits the body to 1 MiB
choices.why: That was lesson 3's `MaxBytesReader`, in boxoffice.

choices.text: It makes Beego decode JSON instead of forms
choices.why: The handler decodes with `json.Unmarshal` itself.

choices.text: It turns off the HTML error pages for every route of the program
choices.why: The HTML 404 still arrived with this setting on.

prompt: `cat -v` shows `^[[1;34m[I]^[[0m` in Beego's log. What are those characters?

choices.text: Bytes of a log file corrupted by two processes writing to it at the same time
choices.why: They are deliberate escape sequences.

choices.text: The id Beego gives each request, so that its lines can be grouped later
choices.why: `[I]` marks the level, information.

choices.text: Terminal colour codes, written though no terminal was watching
choices.why: Right. A log meant for a machine should not contain them.

choices.text: Compressed text
choices.why: Nothing in the log is compressed.

prompt: Match each version to its binary size.
Across the five versions, which measure barely moved?
hint: Three numbers were read off each.

choices.text: The modules in each program's module graph
choices.why: From 0 to 102 besides your own.

choices.text: The non-blank lines of `main.go`
choices.why: Right, from 60 to 75: a framework saved about a dozen lines here.

choices.text: The size in bytes of each binary that `go build` wrote
choices.why: From 9.8 MB to 31.6 MB.

choices.text: The number of routes
choices.why: Every version has the same two, by design.

prompt: According to the lesson, what is the real cost of a framework?

choices.text: The bytes of a larger binary
choices.why: The lesson says explicitly: not the bytes.

choices.text: The extra lines each handler needs
choices.why: The frameworks saved lines rather than adding them.

choices.text: A licence fee
choices.why: All four are free; licences are mentioned only as something to approve.

choices.text: Behaviours you did not choose
choices.why: Right: Gin's 404 for a wrong method, Echo's hidden detail, Beego's HTML page.

prompt: Your team's existing service is written in Gin, and you are adding a second service. What does the lesson advise?
hint: The first sentence of "Which one, if any".

choices.text: Use Gin again
choices.why: Right: consistency inside a codebase is worth more than any row of the table.

choices.text: Switch to Echo, which has fewer modules
choices.why: Fewer modules is one row; the lesson ranks consistency above every row.

choices.text: Move both services to Fiber for its speed
choices.why: Only where its speed has been measured to matter.

choices.text: Write the new one in Beego to get an ORM
choices.why: Beego costs the most to change your mind about.

prompt: How many modules besides the program's own came with the Beego version?
Order the five versions by binary size, smallest first.
trap: Gin carries more modules than Fiber and Echo together.

prompt: A service spends most of each request waiting on a database, and its team knows the standard library and its middleware. Someone proposes Fiber for speed. What is the lesson's answer?

choices.text: Adopt it: fasthttp is faster and nothing else changes
choices.why: The middleware, `httptest` and HTTP/2 all change.

choices.text: Refuse it because Fiber writes errors as text
choices.why: That is a default you change in `fiber.Config`, not the deciding issue.

choices.text: Doubt the speed is felt, and count what leaving `net/http` costs
choices.why: Right. Fiber suits services where its speed has been measured to matter.

choices.text: Adopt it because it has the fewest modules
choices.why: Fiber brings 25; Echo brings 8.
